blocks.text: Most effect bugs come from using an effect for something that is not a side effect at all. Here are the patterns worth un-learning.
3. Resetting state when a prop changes

An effect that sets state which triggers another effect that sets more state produces a cascade of renders that is very hard to follow. Compute what you can in one place, and use an event handler for the rest.
A useful test: if you can answer 'what external system is this synchronising with?' then an effect is right. If you cannot, it probably belongs in a calculation or an event handler.

blocks.title: Write a cleanup-safe subscribe function
blocks.instructions: Complete subscribe so it registers the listener and returns a function that removes it again.

tests.name: The listener is registered
tests.code: var t = { handlers: {}, addEventListener: function (n, f) { this.handlers[n] = f; }, removeEventListener: function (n) { delete this.handlers[n]; } }; subscribe(t, 'x', function () {}); return typeof t.handlers.x === 'function';

tests.name: A cleanup function is returned
tests.code: var t = { handlers: {}, addEventListener: function (n, f) { this.handlers[n] = f; }, removeEventListener: function (n) { delete this.handlers[n]; } }; return typeof subscribe(t, 'x', function () {}) === 'function';

tests.name: Calling cleanup removes the listener
tests.code: var t = { handlers: {}, addEventListener: function (n, f) { this.handlers[n] = f; }, removeEventListener: function (n) { delete this.handlers[n]; } }; var off = subscribe(t, 'x', function () {}); off(); return t.handlers.x === undefined;

blocks.text: An effect can return a function. React calls it before running the effect again, and once more when the component unmounts. Anything the effect started must be stopped there.
A missing cleanup is a memory leak. Timers keep firing, listeners pile up on every re-render, and sockets stay open after the component is gone.
Cleanup runs between updates, not only at the end
With dependencies, the sequence on each change is: run cleanup for the old values, then run the effect with the new ones. That is what keeps the subscription pointing at the right thing.
In development, React Strict Mode mounts each component, runs its effects, cleans them up, and runs them again. It is checking that your cleanup actually undoes the setup.

If double mounting breaks your component - duplicate requests, a doubled counter - the effect is missing cleanup. Strict Mode did not cause the bug, it revealed one that would appear in production the first time the component remounts.
Async work needs guarding: a slow response for an old input must not overwrite a fresh one.
